statement_record.book: The category of sets is cocomplete: it has colimits of all small diagrams.

Class ElementaryTopos (C : Category) := { topos_terminal : @Terminal C; topos_cartesian : @Cartesian C; topos_pullbacks : @HasPullbacks C; topos_closed : @Closed C topos_cartesian; topos_classifier : @SubobjectClassifier C topos_terminal }.  (header, line 20: "An elementary topos is a category with finite limits ... Finite limits are carried EXPLICITLY here as terminal object + binary products + pullbacks")
Theorem Terminal_Limit (C : Category) (F : 0 ⟶ C) : Limit F ↔ @Terminal C.
Theorem Cartesian_Limit (C : Category) : (∀ F : Two_Discrete ⟶ C, Limit F) ↔ @Cartesian C.

"For the finite-completeness clause we package a terminal object together with all pullbacks ([regular_terminal], [regular_pullbacks]). This is the standard economical presentation: binary products are pullbacks over the terminal object, and equalizers are pullbacks of the induced pairings, so a terminal object and pullbacks generate all finite limits."

evidence.intree_statement: (* The binary meet (product object): TwoX is the bottom, TwoY the top. *)  Definition two_meet (x y : TwoObj) : TwoObj := match x with | TwoX => TwoX | TwoY => y end.

(* Binary products on 2 given by meets. *)  Program Instance Two_Cartesian : @Cartesian _2 := {| product_obj := two_meet; fork := two_fork; exl := two_exl; exr := two_exr |}.  Next Obligation. split; intros; try split; apply two_thin. Qed.

(* Product: conjunction. P ∧ Q is the meet, with proj1/proj2 the projections and conj the pairing of two implications. *)  #[export] Program Instance Props_Cartesian : @Cartesian Props := { product_obj := and; fork := fun _ _ _ f g x => conj (f x) (g x); exl := fun _ _ p => proj1 p; exr := fun _ _ p => proj2 p }.

(* Coproduct: disjunction. P ∨ Q is the join, with the injections or_introl/or_intror and case analysis providing the copairing. *)  #[export] Program Instance Props_Cocartesian : @Cocartesian Props := { product_obj := or; ... }.

"In a thin category all parallel morphisms are equal, so every diagram commutes and every coherence condition holds vacuously. Each categorical concept therefore collapses to its order-theoretic shadow, and [Poset] installs the resulting dictionary: ... a product is a meet, and more generally the limit over a subset is its greatest lower bound (nLab, "meet"); a coproduct is a join (Structure/Cocartesian.v)."

statement_record.book: In a preorder P, a product of a family (a_j)_{j∈J} is an object d with d ≤ a_j for all j such that c ≤ a_j for all j implies c ≤ d — i.e. exactly a greatest lower bound (meet); dually a coproduct is exactly a least upper bound (join). Completeness is therefore chiefly useful for large categories and preorders.
statement_record.intree: The identification is realized concretely in two thin categories: on the walking arrow _2, product_obj is literally two_meet with every UMP obligation discharged by two_thin (Instance/Two/Monoidal.v:37,80); on Props (thin, homset equiv := True, so P ~> Q iff P entails Q), product_obj := and and coproduct product_obj := or, commented in-file as 'P ∧ Q is the meet' and 'P ∨ Q is the join' (Instance/Props.v:69,80). Instance/Poset.v:47-53 states the general dictionary as documentation.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker: the general biconditional over an arbitrary preorder is documentation only. The two witnesses are (a) BINARY, not J-indexed — Mac Lane's statement is about a family (a_j)_{j∈J} — and (b) specific to two particular thin categories rather than to Proset P for an arbitrary PreOrder R. No order-theoretic vocabulary (meet, glb, join, lub) is defined anywhere in the tree, so the right-hand side of the identification has no in-tree definiens to compare against.
